title: ‘Tulip mania’ probably wasn’t the disaster the legend says
body: The story goes that in 1637 Dutch tulip bulbs sold for the price of houses, then crashed and ruined the economy. Prices for some rare bulbs really did soar and then collapse in February 1637. But historians such as Anne Goldgar, working through archival records, found little evidence of widespread bankruptcy or wider economic damage; the trade involved a fairly small circle of merchants and artisans.

slides.heading: Where the legend came from
slides.text: Much of the lore traces to moralising pamphlets of the time and to Charles Mackay’s 1841 book Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds.

slides.heading: Why bulbs were pricey
slides.text: The most prized ‘broken’ tulips had flame-like streaks caused, as was found centuries later, by a virus, which made them striking and hard to propagate.

slides.heading: Still debated
slides.text: Some economists, like Peter Garber, argue prices were less irrational than they look; others see a classic bubble. Either way, the crash was short and local.
